claims.text: Premelting and melting behavior of HEA nanoparticles is governed by competition between configurational-entropy-driven bulk stabilization and nanoscale surface-energy-driven destabilization.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the bulk phase of HEA nanoparticles against melting.
Random mixing of multiple metals raises the intrinsic melting point of the nanoparticle bulk.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of HEA nanoparticles promotes surface diffusion and local atomic disorder, causing premelting below the bulk melting temperature.
The nanoparticle-support interface modulates effective surface energy.
Strong nanoparticle-support binding raises the energy barrier for surface-atom mobility.
Strongly anchored nanoparticles should begin surface premelting at a higher temperature than otherwise identical unsupported nanoparticles.
Strongly supported HEA nanoparticles should exhibit a more defined melting point than unsupported nanoparticles.
Defective turbostratic graphite provides numerous nucleation sites for metallic nanoparticle formation.
Metallic nanoparticles can partially intercalate into and root on turbostratic-graphite edge planes, producing high support binding energy.
Strong anchoring to defective turbostratic graphite provides excellent thermal stability to metallic nanoparticles.
HEAs generally consist of five or more principal elements in near-equimolar ratios.
HEA nanoparticles are relevant to catalysis, sensing, and energy-storage applications.
The magnitude of the support-induced premelting or melting shift may depend on nanoparticle composition, size distribution, and support chemistry.
No statistically significant difference in premelting onset or overall melting behavior between supported and unsupported particles would falsify the proposed interfacial-binding control.
